reference.source: Occupational and Environmental Respiratory Medicine reference texts
clinicalPearls: Linked to inhalation of the butter-flavouring agent diacetyl (and its substitute 2,3-pentanedione) in microwave popcorn, flavouring, and food-manufacturing plants
Causes constrictive (obliterative) bronchiolitis, producing fixed airflow obstruction that mimics severe asthma or COPD in a young non-smoker
Symptoms of cough and exertional breathlessness are often insidious and progressive and may not reverse with bronchodilators
Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern; CT typically reveals mosaic attenuation and air trapping on expiratory imaging rather than parenchymal opacities
The chest radiograph is frequently normal or near-normal, which can lead to underdiagnosis
Small-airway scarring narrows and obliterates terminal bronchioles, and established disease is largely irreversible
Recognition of an occupational cluster among flavouring or food-production workers is a critical diagnostic pointer
reference.pathophysiology: Volatile alpha-diketones such as diacetyl, released when heated flavourings are handled, are inhaled and cause direct toxic injury to the epithelium of the small conducting airways. The ensuing inflammation and repair lead to concentric peribronchiolar fibrosis that narrows and ultimately obliterates the lumen of terminal and respiratory bronchioles (constrictive bronchiolitis). Because the injury is confined largely to the small airways with sparing of the surrounding parenchyma, gas exchange may be relatively preserved while airflow obstruction becomes fixed and progressive. The scarring is not reversible, so the emphasis is on early detection and exposure cessation.
additionalDifferentials: Bronchiolitis obliterans after transplantation or connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Spirometry demonstrating fixed airflow obstruction with limited bronchodilator response
High-resolution CT with expiratory views to detect mosaic attenuation and air trapping
Detailed occupational history including flavouring and food-manufacturing exposure
Lung biopsy showing constrictive bronchiolitis when diagnosis is uncertain
Serial lung-function surveillance of exposed workers
redFlags: Rapidly progressive fixed airflow obstruction in a young non-smoker
Continued workplace exposure after symptom onset
Severe irreversible obstruction with respiratory failure
A cluster of affected workers signalling ongoing hazardous exposure
reference.prognosis: Constrictive bronchiolitis from diacetyl is typically irreversible; some patients stabilise after removal from exposure, but others progress to severe disabling airflow obstruction and may require consideration of transplantation.
pitfalls: Mistaking the disease for ordinary asthma and relying on bronchodilators that do not reverse fixed obstruction
Being reassured by a normal chest radiograph and omitting expiratory CT
Missing the occupational history in a young non-smoker with obstruction
Delaying removal from exposure until irreversible damage has occurred
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Immediate and permanent removal from diacetyl and 2,3-pentanedione exposure, with workplace substitution, engineering controls and respiratory protection, as scarring is irreversible and cessation is the only disease-modifying step
Trial of inhaled bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids, recognising that the fixed obstruction of constrictive bronchiolitis usually responds poorly
Pulmonary rehabilitation, smoking cessation and influenza and pneumococcal immunisation to optimise residual respiratory function
Long-term supplemental oxygen for chronic hypoxaemia in advanced disease
Serial spirometry surveillance of the patient and of co-exposed workers to detect progression early
Referral to an occupational lung disease specialist, with formal reporting as an occupational disease
Referral for lung transplantation assessment when obstruction becomes severe and progressive despite exposure cessation
